In a 163-patient Heidelberg cohort, diagnostic criteria were reached in: non-ceruloplasmin-bound serum copper 86.6%, serum ceruloplasmin 88.2%, 24-h urinary copper excretion 87.1%, liver copper content 92.7%, Kayser-Fleischer rings 66.3%, histological chronic liver damage 73%. ATP7B mutation analysis (coding region, excluding exons 2/3/21) detected disease-causing mutations on both chromosomes in 57% of patients, on one chromosome in 29%, and none in 15%.

Wilson disease (WD) is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in ATP7B (chromosome 13q14.3), which encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting P-type ATPase. Loss of ATP7B function impairs biliary copper excretion and copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin, causing progressive toxic copper accumulation, first in the liver and subsequently in the brain, cornea and other organs.

Core clinical picture is polyuria and compensatory polydipsia, with nocturia disrupting sleep. Polyuria of >50 mL/kg body weight per day has been used as a formal inclusion threshold for hypotonic-polyuria diagnostic studies. Dehydration/hypernatremia risk rises sharply if thirst sensation is impaired (adipsic patients), water access is restricted, or the patient is an infant/unconscious and cannot self-regulate intake. Hereditary nephrogenic DI classically presents in the first year of life with polyuria, chronic dehydration, and hypernatremia.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is excretion of large volumes of hypotonic (dilute) urine. Central DI results from deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to AVP action at the V2 receptor or the AQP2 water channel in the collecting duct. Gestational DI is caused by excess circulating placental vasopressinase (a cystine aminopeptidase) that accelerates AVP degradation. All three are distinct from primary polydipsia, in which AVP secretion/action is normal but water intake is excessive (a subgroup with an abnormally low thirst threshold is termed dipsogenic DI).

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is excretion of large volumes of hypotonic (dilute) urine. Central DI results from deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to AVP action at the V2 receptor or the AQP2 water channel in the collecting duct. Gestational DI is caused by excess circulating placental vasopressinase (a cystine aminopeptidase) that accelerates AVP degradation. All three are distinct from primary polydipsia, in which AVP secretion/action is normal but water intake is excessive (a subgroup with an abnormally low thirst threshold is termed dipsogenic DI).

Fibromuscular dysplasia is formally defined and classified (multifocal 'string of beads' vs focal/unifocal disease) with contemporary diagnostic and management criteria for renal, cerebrovascular, and other arterial beds in adults; explicitly a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arterial disease distinct from atherosclerotic RAS.

Noninvasive imaging (duplex ultrasound, CTA, MRA) is used first-line to detect RAS and select patients for confirmatory catheter angiography, which remains the reference standard. A validated clinical prediction rule can also flag which hypertensive patients most need imaging.

Renovascular disease is described as the prototype of angiotensin-dependent (RAAS-driven) hypertension: reduced renal perfusion pressure sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus drives renin release, angiotensin II generation, systemic vasoconstriction, and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention. Atherosclerotic RAS is stated to be the most common type of renovascular disease overall.

Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is narrowing of one or both main renal arteries (or their branches), reducing renal perfusion pressure and triggering renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation. Two distinct arteriopathies account for almost all cases: atherosclerotic RAS (~90% of cases; older patients, ostial/proximal-third lesion, part of diffuse systemic atherosclerosis) and fibromuscular dysplasia, FMD (~10%; non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy of mid-to-distal renal artery, classic 'string-of-beads' angiographic pattern, strong female/younger-age predominance).

A genuinely central and clinically important feature of prostate cancer, unlike most other solid cancers, is that a very large proportion of histologically detectable disease is truly indolent and would never cause symptoms or death if left undetected -- autopsy series cited by NCI PDQ estimate that approximately 30% to 70% of men over age 60 harbour clinically indolent prostate cancer at death from unrelated causes, a real and substantial reservoir of disease that PSA-era screening and biopsy readily detect but that carries no true clinical threat in most of these men. This is the direct real basis of the overdiagnosis/overtreatment tension that runs through this entire disease's diagnostic and management framework (see diagnostic_framework.psa_screening_controversy and clinical_takeaway below): Grade Group 1 (Gleason <=6) disease in particular is now managed very differently from higher-grade disease specifically because of this indolent-biology reality, in contrast to most other cancers where any detected malignancy is treated promptly.

Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising overwhelmingly from the glandular (acinar) epithelial cells of the peripheral zone of the prostate, and its growth and survival are fundamentally androgen-dependent: androgens (testosterone and its more potent intraprostatic metabolite dihydrotestosterone) bind the androgen receptor (AR) in prostate epithelial cells, driving AR-mediated transcriptional programs that promote proliferation and survival of both normal and malignant prostatic epithelium. b_unique_terms: The real, documented harms weighed against PSA screening's modest mortality benefit include: overdiagnosis of clinically insignificant cancer (an estimated 20-50% of screen-detected cancers may never have caused symptoms in a man's lifetime); biopsy-related complications (infection, pain, hematuria, rarely sepsis); psychological harm from false-positive results; and substantial treatment-related morbidity in men who are treated -- about 1 in 5 men undergoing radical prostatectomy develop long-term urinary incontinence and roughly 2 in 3 experience erectile dysfunction. USPSTF estimates the absolute mortality benefit of screening at approximately 1.3 deaths averted per 1,000 men screened over 13 years, a real but small number that must be weighed against these harms on an individual basis.
Neoplasm of the central nervous system

A genuinely central and clinically important feature of prostate cancer, unlike most other solid cancers, is that a very large proportion of histologically detectable disease is truly indolent and would never cause symptoms or death if left undetected -- autopsy series cited by NCI PDQ estimate that approximately 30% to 70% of men over age 60 harbour clinically indolent prostate cancer at death from unrelated causes, a real and substantial reservoir of disease that PSA-era screening and biopsy readily detect but that carries no true clinical threat in most of these men. This is the direct real basis of the overdiagnosis/overtreatment tension that runs through this entire disease's diagnostic and management framework (see diagnostic_framework.psa_screening_controversy and clinical_takeaway below): Grade Group 1 (Gleason <=6) disease in particular is now managed very differently from higher-grade disease specifically because of this indolent-biology reality, in contrast to most other cancers where any detected malignancy is treated promptly.

Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising overwhelmingly from the glandular (acinar) epithelial cells of the peripheral zone of the prostate, and its growth and survival are fundamentally androgen-dependent: androgens (testosterone and its more potent intraprostatic metabolite dihydrotestosterone) bind the androgen receptor (AR) in prostate epithelial cells, driving AR-mediated transcriptional programs that promote proliferation and survival of both normal and malignant prostatic epithelium. This androgen-dependence is the real, direct mechanistic basis for the entire treatment paradigm in intermediate/high-risk and advanced disease: androgen-deprivation therapy (surgical or medical castration, GnRH agonists/antagonists, and androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors) works by cutting off this same growth-driving signal, and eventual disease progression on such therapy (castration-resistant prostate cancer) reflects the tumour evolving AR-pathway workarounds (e.g., AR amplification, AR splice variants) rather than becoming androgen-independent in an absolute sense.

Digital rectal examination (DRE) -- a gloved, lubricated finger inserted into the rectum to palpate the prostate for asymmetry, induration, or a discrete nodule -- remains a real, low-cost adjunct to PSA testing, but its independent contribution to mortality reduction has not been established with the same randomized-trial rigor as PSA, and it is not recommended as a stand-alone population screening test by USPSTF.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is excretion of large volumes of hypotonic (dilute) urine. Central DI results from deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to AVP action at the V2 receptor or the AQP2 water channel in the collecting duct. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the real procedure of choice for both diagnosing and treating a suspected malignant testicular mass, performed via an inguinal (not transscrotal) approach specifically to avoid disrupting the lymphatic drainage of the scrotum -- real studies show a small but statistically significant increase in local recurrence with a transscrotal approach (2.9% versus 0.4%) due to the real risk of local tumor dissemination/seeding into inguinal lymph nodes that a transscrotal incision creates.

Three real serum tumor markers guide diagnosis, staging, and prognosis, and must be measured before orchiectomy to establish a baseline: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas and is produced exclusively by nonseminomatous elements (yolk sac tumor and teratoma components specifically) -- seminomas do not produce AFP, so a real elevated AFP in an apparently pure seminoma indicates occult NSGCT component and must change management. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is elevated in a real approximately 14% of men with stage I pure seminoma preoperatively, in about one-half of men with metastatic seminoma, and in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas, with choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma the specific NSGCT histologies most strongly associated with beta-hCG production. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is produced by both seminomas and nonseminomas, is of real unclear independent prognostic significance in early-stage disease, but is a real significant predictor of survival in metastatic NSGCT and is incorporated into the S-stage and IGCCCG risk classification below.

Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

Scrotal ultrasonography is the real, gold-standard initial imaging test for any suspected testicular mass, allowing reliable differentiation between an intratesticular lesion (which must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise) and an extratesticular lesion (hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst, etc.), which is real-world overwhelmingly benign.

For tumours found to be high-grade or invasive on TURBT, cross-sectional imaging (CT urography/CT of the abdomen and pelvis) and chest imaging are added to assess for upper-tract urothelial disease, extravesical extension, nodal disease, and distant metastasis -- staged imaging is reserved for higher-risk disease rather than applied uniformly to every newly diagnosed low-grade tumour, reflecting the low metastatic potential of low-grade NMIBC.

Bladder cancer is fundamentally divided by depth of invasion into the muscularis propria, and this split is the real, central organizing fact of the entire disease: approximately 70% to 80% of newly diagnosed patients present with non-muscle-invasive disease (stage Ta, Tis/carcinoma in situ, or T1 -- confined to mucosa/lamina propria), while the remaining 20% to 30% present with muscle-invasive disease (T2 or higher) at initial diagnosis. Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is managed with organ-preserving transurethral resection plus intravesical therapy and surveillance, whereas muscle-invasive disease (MIBC) typically requires radical cystectomy or trimodality bladder-preserving therapy given its much higher risk of nodal/distant spread -- so this Ta/Tis/T1 versus T2+ distinction, not tumour grade alone, is what principally determines the management pathway.

Real dose-response data: the average threshold alcohol intake associated with liver injury is approximately 40-60 g/day (roughly 3-5 standard drinks) in men but only approximately 20 g/day (fewer than 2 standard drinks) in women -- a real, clinically important sex difference (women develop alcohol-related liver injury, including cirrhosis, faster and at lower cumulative doses than men for a similar drinking history). A daily intake above approximately 60 g/day in men and above approximately 20 g/day in women significantly increases cirrhosis risk specifically (not just any liver injury), and separate meta-analyses report a real threshold effect for significantly increased cirrhosis risk above approximately 24 g/day. In patients with chronic hepatitis B, every additional 12 g/day of alcohol (~1 drink) was associated with an approximately 6.2% relative increase in cirrhosis risk compared with non-drinkers -- a real, clinically important alcohol-viral-hepatitis interaction/co-factor effect. Daily drinking (versus binge-pattern drinking) appears more harmful for cumulative liver injury.

Migraine aura is caused by cortical spreading depression (CSD, the phenomenon first described by Leao) - a slowly propagating (3-5 mm/min) wave of intense neuronal and glial depolarisation across the cortex, followed by a longer-lasting wave of suppressed cortical activity, accompanied by transient changes in cerebral blood flow (initial hyperaemia, then prolonged oligaemia) and massive transmembrane ionic and metabolic flux. The spreading depolarisation wavefront corresponds spatially and temporally to the march of aura symptoms (e.g. the expanding visual scintillating scotoma), and CSD can activate trigeminovascular afferents and upregulate CGRP synthesis in trigeminal ganglion neurons, providing a mechanistic link between aura and the subsequent headache phase.

Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

Scrotal ultrasonography is the real, gold-standard initial imaging test for any suspected testicular mass, allowing reliable differentiation between an intratesticular lesion (which must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise) and an extratesticular lesion (hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst, etc.), which is real-world overwhelmingly benign.

Migraine aura is caused by cortical spreading depression (CSD, the phenomenon first described by Leao) - a slowly propagating (3-5 mm/min) wave of intense neuronal and glial depolarisation across the cortex, followed by a longer-lasting wave of suppressed cortical activity, accompanied by transient changes in cerebral blood flow (initial hyperaemia, then prolonged oligaemia) and massive transmembrane ionic and metabolic flux. The spreading depolarisation wavefront corresponds spatially and temporally to the march of aura symptoms (e.g. the expanding visual scintillating scotoma), and CSD can activate trigeminovascular afferents and upregulate CGRP synthesis in trigeminal ganglion neurons, providing a mechanistic link between aura and the subsequent headache phase.

Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a neuropeptide stored in and released from trigeminal C-fibres, is a key mediator of migraine pain: it is a potent vasodilator of intracranial vessels and transmits vascular nociception via CGRP receptors expressed on trigeminal A-delta fibres; plasma CGRP rises during spontaneous and induced migraine attacks and normalises with successful treatment, and intravenous CGRP infusion can trigger migraine-like attacks in susceptible individuals. This mechanistic role is the direct basis for the newest migraine drug class - small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonists (gepants) and monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor - which are effective for both acute treatment and prevention.

Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the real procedure of choice for both diagnosing and treating a suspected malignant testicular mass, performed via an inguinal (not transscrotal) approach specifically to avoid disrupting the lymphatic drainage of the scrotum -- real studies show a small but statistically significant increase in local recurrence with a transscrotal approach (2.9% versus 0.4%) due to the real risk of local tumor dissemination/seeding into inguinal lymph nodes that a transscrotal incision creates.

Three real serum tumor markers guide diagnosis, staging, and prognosis, and must be measured before orchiectomy to establish a baseline: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas and is produced exclusively by nonseminomatous elements (yolk sac tumor and teratoma components specifically) -- seminomas do not produce AFP, so a real elevated AFP in an apparently pure seminoma indicates occult NSGCT component and must change management. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is elevated in a real approximately 14% of men with stage I pure seminoma preoperatively, in about one-half of men with metastatic seminoma, and in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas, with choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma the specific NSGCT histologies most strongly associated with beta-hCG production. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is produced by both seminomas and nonseminomas, is of real unclear independent prognostic significance in early-stage disease, but is a real significant predictor of survival in metastatic NSGCT and is incorporated into the S-stage and IGCCCG risk classification below.

Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

Scrotal ultrasonography is the real, gold-standard initial imaging test for any suspected testicular mass, allowing reliable differentiation between an intratesticular lesion (which must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise) and an extratesticular lesion (hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst, etc.), which is real-world overwhelmingly benign.

Fibromuscular dysplasia is formally defined and classified (multifocal 'string of beads' vs focal/unifocal disease) with contemporary diagnostic and management criteria for renal, cerebrovascular, and other arterial beds in adults; explicitly a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arterial disease distinct from atherosclerotic RAS.

Noninvasive imaging (duplex ultrasound, CTA, MRA) is used first-line to detect RAS and select patients for confirmatory catheter angiography, which remains the reference standard. A validated clinical prediction rule can also flag which hypertensive patients most need imaging.

Renovascular disease is described as the prototype of angiotensin-dependent (RAAS-driven) hypertension: reduced renal perfusion pressure sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus drives renin release, angiotensin II generation, systemic vasoconstriction, and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention. Atherosclerotic RAS is stated to be the most common type of renovascular disease overall.

Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is narrowing of one or both main renal arteries (or their branches), reducing renal perfusion pressure and triggering renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation. Two distinct arteriopathies account for almost all cases: atherosclerotic RAS (~90% of cases; older patients, ostial/proximal-third lesion, part of diffuse systemic atherosclerosis) and fibromuscular dysplasia, FMD (~10%; non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy of mid-to-distal renal artery, classic 'string-of-beads' angiographic pattern, strong female/younger-age predominance).

a_unique_terms: Core clinical picture is polyuria and compensatory polydipsia, with nocturia disrupting sleep. Polyuria of >50 mL/kg body weight per day has been used as a formal inclusion threshold for hypotonic-polyuria diagnostic studies. Dehydration/hypernatremia risk rises sharply if thirst sensation is impaired (adipsic patients), water access is restricted, or the patient is an infant/unconscious and cannot self-regulate intake. Hereditary nephrogenic DI classically presents in the first year of life with polyuria, chronic dehydration, and hypernatremia.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is excretion of large volumes of hypotonic (dilute) urine. Central DI results from deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to AVP action at the V2 receptor or the AQP2 water channel in the collecting duct. Gestational DI is caused by excess circulating placental vasopressinase (a cystine aminopeptidase) that accelerates AVP degradation. All three are distinct from primary polydipsia, in which AVP secretion/action is normal but water intake is excessive (a subgroup with an abnormally low thirst threshold is termed dipsogenic DI).

A genuinely central and clinically important feature of prostate cancer, unlike most other solid cancers, is that a very large proportion of histologically detectable disease is truly indolent and would never cause symptoms or death if left undetected -- autopsy series cited by NCI PDQ estimate that approximately 30% to 70% of men over age 60 harbour clinically indolent prostate cancer at death from unrelated causes, a real and substantial reservoir of disease that PSA-era screening and biopsy readily detect but that carries no true clinical threat in most of these men. This is the direct real basis of the overdiagnosis/overtreatment tension that runs through this entire disease's diagnostic and management framework (see diagnostic_framework.psa_screening_controversy and clinical_takeaway below): Grade Group 1 (Gleason <=6) disease in particular is now managed very differently from higher-grade disease specifically because of this indolent-biology reality, in contrast to most other cancers where any detected malignancy is treated promptly.

Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising overwhelmingly from the glandular (acinar) epithelial cells of the peripheral zone of the prostate, and its growth and survival are fundamentally androgen-dependent: androgens (testosterone and its more potent intraprostatic metabolite dihydrotestosterone) bind the androgen receptor (AR) in prostate epithelial cells, driving AR-mediated transcriptional programs that promote proliferation and survival of both normal and malignant prostatic epithelium. This androgen-dependence is the real, direct mechanistic basis for the entire treatment paradigm in intermediate/high-risk and advanced disease: androgen-deprivation therapy (surgical or medical castration, GnRH agonists/antagonists, and androgen-receptor-pathway inhibitors) works by cutting off this same growth-driving signal, and eventual disease progression on such therapy (castration-resistant prostate cancer) reflects the tumour evolving AR-pathway workarounds (e.g., AR amplification, AR splice variants) rather than becoming androgen-independent in an absolute sense.

Digital rectal examination (DRE) -- a gloved, lubricated finger inserted into the rectum to palpate the prostate for asymmetry, induration, or a discrete nodule -- remains a real, low-cost adjunct to PSA testing, but its independent contribution to mortality reduction has not been established with the same randomized-trial rigor as PSA, and it is not recommended as a stand-alone population screening test by USPSTF.

Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the real procedure of choice for both diagnosing and treating a suspected malignant testicular mass, performed via an inguinal (not transscrotal) approach specifically to avoid disrupting the lymphatic drainage of the scrotum -- real studies show a small but statistically significant increase in local recurrence with a transscrotal approach (2.9% versus 0.4%) due to the real risk of local tumor dissemination/seeding into inguinal lymph nodes that a transscrotal incision creates.

Three real serum tumor markers guide diagnosis, staging, and prognosis, and must be measured before orchiectomy to establish a baseline: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas and is produced exclusively by nonseminomatous elements (yolk sac tumor and teratoma components specifically) -- seminomas do not produce AFP, so a real elevated AFP in an apparently pure seminoma indicates occult NSGCT component and must change management. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is elevated in a real approximately 14% of men with stage I pure seminoma preoperatively, in about one-half of men with metastatic seminoma, and in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas, with choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma the specific NSGCT histologies most strongly associated with beta-hCG production. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is produced by both seminomas and nonseminomas, is of real unclear independent prognostic significance in early-stage disease, but is a real significant predictor of survival in metastatic NSGCT and is incorporated into the S-stage and IGCCCG risk classification below.

Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

Scrotal ultrasonography is the real, gold-standard initial imaging test for any suspected testicular mass, allowing reliable differentiation between an intratesticular lesion (which must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise) and an extratesticular lesion (hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst, etc.), which is real-world overwhelmingly benign.

Prostate cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising overwhelmingly from the glandular (acinar) epithelial cells of the peripheral zone of the prostate, and its growth and survival are fundamentally androgen-dependent: androgens (testosterone and its more potent intraprostatic metabolite dihydrotestosterone) bind the androgen receptor (AR) in prostate epithelial cells, driving AR-mediated transcriptional programs that promote proliferation and survival of both normal and malignant prostatic epithelium. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the real procedure of choice for both diagnosing and treating a suspected malignant testicular mass, performed via an inguinal (not transscrotal) approach specifically to avoid disrupting the lymphatic drainage of the scrotum -- real studies show a small but statistically significant increase in local recurrence with a transscrotal approach (2.9% versus 0.4%) due to the real risk of local tumor dissemination/seeding into inguinal lymph nodes that a transscrotal incision creates.

Three real serum tumor markers guide diagnosis, staging, and prognosis, and must be measured before orchiectomy to establish a baseline: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas and is produced exclusively by nonseminomatous elements (yolk sac tumor and teratoma components specifically) -- seminomas do not produce AFP, so a real elevated AFP in an apparently pure seminoma indicates occult NSGCT component and must change management. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is elevated in a real approximately 14% of men with stage I pure seminoma preoperatively, in about one-half of men with metastatic seminoma, and in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas, with choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma the specific NSGCT histologies most strongly associated with beta-hCG production. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is produced by both seminomas and nonseminomas, is of real unclear independent prognostic significance in early-stage disease, but is a real significant predictor of survival in metastatic NSGCT and is incorporated into the S-stage and IGCCCG risk classification below.

Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

Scrotal ultrasonography is the real, gold-standard initial imaging test for any suspected testicular mass, allowing reliable differentiation between an intratesticular lesion (which must be presumed malignant until proven otherwise) and an extratesticular lesion (hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst, etc.), which is real-world overwhelmingly benign.

Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) is elevated in a real approximately 14% of men with stage I pure seminoma preoperatively, in about one-half of men with metastatic seminoma, and in a real 40% to 60% of men with nonseminomas, with choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma the specific NSGCT histologies most strongly associated with beta-hCG production. Testicular cancer is a real malignant neoplasm arising from the germinal epithelium of the testis; germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for approximately 95% of all testicular malignancies. The WHO classification divides malignant testicular GCTs into two clinically fundamental categories that drive the entire treatment paradigm: seminoma (a single pure histology, real-world approximately 40% of GCTs) and nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma, alone or -- most commonly -- as real mixed germ cell tumors combining more than one of these patterns, real-world approximately 60% of GCTs). This seminoma-versus-NSGCT split is genuinely important, not a minor pathological footnote, because seminomas show real superior chemosensitivity and radiosensitivity with a lower propensity for distant metastasis, whereas nonseminomas often contain teratomatous elements that are real-world resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, necessitating surgical resection (post-chemotherapy retroperitoneal lymph node dissection) for cure -- the same real distinction is why tumor markers, staging, and treatment selection below are organized around this split rather than around a single unified 'testicular cancer' category. Within NSGCT, choriocarcinoma carries the real highest metastatic potential and teratoma the real lowest.

a_unique_terms: More than 90% of bladder cancers in the US are urothelial carcinoma (also called transitional cell carcinoma), arising from the urothelium lining the bladder; squamous cell carcinoma accounts for about 2% to 7% (higher where chronic irritation/Schistosoma haematobium infection is endemic) and adenocarcinoma for about 2%. This histologic predominance is the real basis for urothelial-carcinoma-directed diagnostic and treatment pathways being the default approach to a newly diagnosed bladder tumour.
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder

For tumours found to be high-grade or invasive on TURBT, cross-sectional imaging (CT urography/CT of the abdomen and pelvis) and chest imaging are added to assess for upper-tract urothelial disease, extravesical extension, nodal disease, and distant metastasis -- staged imaging is reserved for higher-risk disease rather than applied uniformly to every newly diagnosed low-grade tumour, reflecting the low metastatic potential of low-grade NMIBC.

Bladder cancer is fundamentally divided by depth of invasion into the muscularis propria, and this split is the real, central organizing fact of the entire disease: approximately 70% to 80% of newly diagnosed patients present with non-muscle-invasive disease (stage Ta, Tis/carcinoma in situ, or T1 -- confined to mucosa/lamina propria), while the remaining 20% to 30% present with muscle-invasive disease (T2 or higher) at initial diagnosis. Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) is managed with organ-preserving transurethral resection plus intravesical therapy and surveillance, whereas muscle-invasive disease (MIBC) typically requires radical cystectomy or trimodality bladder-preserving therapy given its much higher risk of nodal/distant spread -- so this Ta/Tis/T1 versus T2+ distinction, not tumour grade alone, is what principally determines the management pathway.
Painless gross or microscopic hematuria (cardinal symptom)

Cystoscopy (direct endoscopic visualization of the bladder urothelium via a scope passed through the urethra) is the real, most useful and standard diagnostic test when bladder cancer is suspected; radiologic studies such as CT or ultrasound lack sufficient sensitivity to reliably detect or exclude bladder tumours. When a lesion is seen, the standard diagnostic-and-initial-treatment procedure is transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), which resects the visible tumour, allows histologic grading and determination of depth of invasion (T-stage), and is therefore both diagnostic and the first therapeutic step; bimanual examination under anesthesia is performed alongside TURBT to assess for a palpable mass suggesting extravesical extension.

a_unique_terms: Core clinical picture is polyuria and compensatory polydipsia, with nocturia disrupting sleep. Polyuria of >50 mL/kg body weight per day has been used as a formal inclusion threshold for hypotonic-polyuria diagnostic studies. Dehydration/hypernatremia risk rises sharply if thirst sensation is impaired (adipsic patients), water access is restricted, or the patient is an infant/unconscious and cannot self-regulate intake. Hereditary nephrogenic DI classically presents in the first year of life with polyuria, chronic dehydration, and hypernatremia.

Diabetes insipidus (DI) is excretion of large volumes of hypotonic (dilute) urine. Central DI results from deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (AVP) by the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary. Nephrogenic DI results from renal resistance to AVP action at the V2 receptor or the AQP2 water channel in the collecting duct. Gestational DI is caused by excess circulating placental vasopressinase (a cystine aminopeptidase) that accelerates AVP degradation. All three are distinct from primary polydipsia, in which AVP secretion/action is normal but water intake is excessive (a subgroup with an abnormally low thirst threshold is termed dipsogenic DI).
